lesson.title: Hands Off the Hemisphere: Monroe Draws a Line
lesson.summary: In an 1823 message to Congress, President Monroe warned Europe against further colonization or intervention in the Americas, a confident statement of national ambition that outran the country's actual military power at the time.
lesson.body:
On December 2, 1823, President James Monroe delivered his annual message to Congress and included a passage on foreign policy that later became known as the Monroe Doctrine. In it, the United States declared that the American continents were no longer open to European colonization and that any European attempt to interfere with the newly independent nations of Latin America would be viewed as a threat to the peace and safety of the United States.

The statement responded to a specific moment. Over the previous fifteen years, most of Spain's colonies in the Americas had fought their way to independence, led by figures such as Simon Bolivar in South America and Jose de San Martin in the southern cone. American leaders sympathized with these new republics and worried that European powers might try to help Spain reclaim its lost colonies. That fear centered on the Holy Alliance, an agreement among Russia, Austria, and Prussia to support monarchy and suppress republican revolutions in Europe, which some feared might extend its reach across the Atlantic.

A second, less remembered concern involved Russia, which in 1821 issued a decree, sometimes called the Ukase of 1821, asserting territorial and trading claims along the Pacific coast of North America stretching down toward Oregon. Monroe's message addressed this threat too, warning European powers generally against establishing new colonies anywhere in the hemisphere.

Secretary of State John Quincy Adams shaped much of the doctrine's substance and pushed for a stronger, more independent stance than Britain had proposed. The British foreign secretary, George Canning, had suggested a joint British American statement against European intervention in Latin America, since Britain wanted open access to Latin American trade too, but Adams argued that the United States should speak for itself rather than appear as a junior partner to the Royal Navy. The doctrine also fit naturally with the nationalist mood of the Era of Good Feelings, expressing a confident, independent posture as the United States began to see itself as a future hemispheric power.

At the time, the United States had neither the navy nor the diplomatic weight to enforce the doctrine on its own, and it was really the British navy's interest in open Latin American markets that discouraged any European reconquest in these years. The doctrine mattered less as an immediate policy than as a statement of American ambition. Later generations of American leaders invoked and expanded it, most famously when Theodore Roosevelt added his Roosevelt Corollary in 1904, claiming the United States had the right to intervene in Latin American affairs to prevent European intervention, turning Monroe's defensive warning into a far more assertive claim of hemispheric authority.
